body: The desk lamp in 412 is bent as low as its neck will go, so the light stays in one circle on the desk and off Theo, who went to sleep at eleven with his face to the wall and the navy robe spread over his blanket for extra. In the circle is Lena’s paper. Hale swapped them down the seminar table this afternoon: eight pages, stapled at a perfect forty-five degrees, with footnotes, and a title page that doesn’t waste anybody’s time.

body.title: M. Broussard — PHIL 9H — YES
body.text:
WHETHER A PROMISE BINDS WHEN ITS REASON IS GONE: YES

A promise is made to a person, not to a reason. When the reason goes, the person is still standing there.

. . .

Take Ruth, since the other side won’t. By the end of the first chapter every reason she had is buried in Moab: the husband, his brother, his father, any hope of sons. Naomi says so herself, in the road, and tells both her daughters-in-law to go home. That is the only honest door out of a promise: the person it was made to, opening it, to your face. Naomi holds it open with both hands. Orpah kisses her and goes, and Scripture doesn’t say one unkind word about Orpah, and neither will I. Ruth won’t go. *Quocumque perrexeris, pergam.* She isn’t confused about the facts. She has buried the facts. She has only noticed the one that’s left, which is that Naomi is still standing in the road. The reasons were never what she promised. They were only why. (p. 5)

body: He reads all eight pages and every footnote, including one that consists of the single word *Obviously*. It’s better than his. It isn’t close. At the bottom of page five he sits back until the desk chair creaks, and Theo says something in his sleep, and goes quiet again.

The RAZR is shut by the lamp. Nothing from SKYE (MISFIT) today; she said Tuesday. He opens it and types *my grandmother fell*, and looks at that on the little screen, and takes it back out a letter at a time. He’ll tell her when he can see her face.

Hale wants margins. Jack uncaps a pen — blue; Lena has all the red ink in Delgado — and turns to page eight, to the place where she stops being right and starts being finished. There’s an inch of white down the side of it.

response: He writes it small, in his square capitals, so it’ll fit in the inch.

response: At midnight he goes down two flights of the east stairs in his socks with the eight pages, and slides them under 217’s door until only the corner with the staple is showing, and then pushes that under too, with one finger.

response: The first sentence goes down fast. Over the second his pen stops, and he nearly strikes it through, and leaves it.

body: Somebody’s roller bag goes down the fourth-floor hall at five past seven, ticking over every seam in the linoleum, the first of the floor going home. When it’s gone Jack opens his eyes, and his own paper is on the floor inside the door, folded once, half under one of Theo’s loafers. He never heard it come.
Her red runs across his title page, over the NO, in a hand that leans forward like it’s late for something.

body.title: J. Costigan — PHIL 9H — NO
body.text:
Best thing you’ve written for him. You don’t believe one sentence of it. He’ll know.
Neither do I. —L.

body: Theo sleeps through it. Jack lies back down with the paper on his chest, folded the way she folded it, and listens to the second roller bag go by.

s14.slug: TUESDAY · 12:10 PM · ST. BRENDAN’S → THE GROVE
body: Father Osei says the 12:10 in red. The martyrs of Vietnam, a hundred and seventeen of them; he gives them one sentence before the Gloria — bishops and priests and catechists, and two soldiers who were ordered to walk across a crucifix and wouldn’t — and then a second: “Some of us will not walk across the quad for Him. Pray for us also.” A dozen people sit in the blue light under the hull, and at the ends of three of the pews there are roller bags parked with their handles up. Somewhere in San Jose, Kevin said this morning, his mother reads eleven of the names.

Jack caught Osei at the sacristy door before Mass with an index card. Osei read it once, put it inside his book, and gripped Jack’s arm above the elbow, a doctor’s grip, and by the time he let go the entrance hymn had started, so Jack took the last pew on the right rather than walk up the aisle in the middle of it. Lena is in the fourth pew on the right, alone, with her bag on the end. Across the aisle, in the fourth on the left, Becca kneels beside Joey Abruzzo.
At the Prayers of the Faithful Osei does the Church and the Pope, the persecuted, and everybody who will be on the roads and in the air this week. Then he opens the book and takes out the card.
“For Carmela Rinaldi,” he reads, “in the hospital in Youngstown, Ohio.”
“Lord, hear our prayer,” say twelve people and Jack.

Her name goes up under the hull along with the Pope’s. Across the aisle Becca’s head comes up out of her hands. And Lena, who has known since yesterday afternoon, turns around in her pew anyway, all the way around, and finds him in the back, and keeps him until Osei has moved on to the dead. Then she faces the altar again.

The Grove after Mass is eucalyptus bark lying across the path in long curls, and the smell the trees give off when the sun has been on them since ten. Lena waits for him under them with the LG open in her hand. Her voice is most of the way back, with a crack still running down the middle of it.

“Mémère called at seven,” she says. “She’s lighting a candle for your nonna. Tonight, at St. Bernard’s, after the rosary. But she wants the whole name.” And then, in Mémère’s French: “*La moitié d’un nom, c’est la moitié d’une chandelle.* Half a name is half a candle. I tried to tell her Carmela was plenty. She said, Carmela *what*.”
“Carmela Rinaldi,” Jack says.

Lena types it with both thumbs on the little keyboard, letter by letter, into a text to her Tante Claudine in Lafayette, who has the job of driving Mémère to St. Bernard’s and holding the lighter. Then she reads it back to him to be sure, *Carmela Rinaldi*, in a New Orleans that does things to the vowels Nonna would object to and then forgive.

body.text: “And she says your nonna raised a boy with manners,” Lena adds, sending it, “so she’s owed.”
“Who drove her?” “My dad.” He gives it a breath. “Sober.” “Good,” Lena says — and nothing else.

body: Her flight is first thing tomorrow. Julian is driving her. “He says he likes airports at that hour,” she says. “I told him that’s a character flaw, and I’d pray for him.”

Down the path Becca comes out of St. Brendan’s side door with her clipboard on her hip, headed for Portolá. She lifts a hand to them, small, and keeps going. Lena waves back big, with the phone still in it.

It buzzes in her hand before Becca is out of sight. Lena reads it and laughs, crack and all, and turns the screen so he can see Tante Claudine’s answer: *Done. Mama says Carmela goes ahead of the Saints’ secondary. That is an honor. Last year it was the levees.*

journal.title: Lena Broussard
journal.text: New Orleans. Two seventeen. Classics. Hale paired us for the semester. Makes a roux like she’s taking a vow and expects you to keep up. Her father sells Gulf shrimp — Broussard’s Seafood, Banks Street. Boyfriend: Wes Arceneaux — Tulane, civil engineering, the boat at sixteen. Calls at 8:04 on the dot. Her grandmother, Lucille Guidry, died in the storm in ’05; they buried her in November, in the good dress. The medal came back to her mother in a plastic bag. She has never asked her mother one question. The year after, she went to Mass every morning to yell at God, and somewhere in there it stopped being a fight. Paints a mean fleur-de-lis. Said hi to Danny. Says she’s going to be defense. Walked her home the long way from Pi Lam: the beach, the creek, the tower, the Commons, the Lagoon bench. Wes calls from somewhere loud lately; her brother Luc is with him. She’s decided not to notice. The Tuesday of the wake he called on the dot, from his room. He came for Columbus Day weekend to see the Pacific. She’d told him it’s a threat. He touched it at two in the morning. Came to Marisol for the money, she says — Notre Dame gave her half. Went to Hale’s office to tell him he was wrong about who gets to forgive. Cried for Anders on the roof and didn’t give an inch. Stayed till the chimes. There’s a sentence she hasn’t finished. Her middle name is Thérèse; October first is her feast. She erased *Show Lena* out of the Hopkins herself, so Danny could have it. At midnight I gave her *Story of a Soul* with my margins in it, and she wouldn’t let me erase a word. On the beach she asked if I know what I’m doing. I don’t. She laughed. At the elevator: ‘That was a terrible thing to be glad about.’ Brought Wes to everything. Wouldn’t walk past the last house on Seacliff toward the Point; said she was cold. At the stove she gave Becca the spoon. Monday night, two floors down, on the phone to New Orleans: ‘He’s my friend, Wes.’ Plays the piano in the Delgado basement — the one nobody admits to playing. Two years at the Rosary. At five in the morning she played the Saints on the Ferrer carillon with her fists, one bell flat, and said it wasn’t flat, it was New Orleans. Wes told her what I said on the beach, and what I didn’t. On a motel porch above Lucia at three in the morning she told me I can’t say her name like that. She asked what I decided. Not to be the one who wrecks anything, I said. She said okay. Then: me neither. Bought her Mémère a fruitcake from the monks, in exact change. ‘A girl writes the thing she wants first, Youngstown.’ Halloween: Flannery O’Connor, with a stuffed peacock tagged 57. Andalusia. She wouldn’t go past the last house on Seacliff, not even for Laney. ‘I came as her. I never said she was right.’ In the last minute of the extra hour, she put my hat back on. All Souls: she wrote her grandmother’s name in the book, and Nora Calloway’s. Nora was her host at Preview Weekend, in April. That night Wes ended it, on the phone, on the east stairs. He stopped going to Mass in September. There’s a ring. She knew something in September and decided not to notice — she says she’s good at it. At six in the morning she asked me what I’m going to do. She wrote Hale twelve pages in the spring of ’08, two years after the year she yelled at God. She’s had the same postcard the whole time. She knew mine on the porch. She had a house picked out on Zimple Street. A fig tree. She’d picked the paint. Veterans Day, on the bench above Campus Point: St. Martin gave the beggar half his cloak; she says everybody forgets the beggar took it. No. 9 for the reliquary. Friday the 13th, under the eucalyptus, in the middle of a sentence about monarchs: Julian asked her to dinner. So. Thursday night in the basement she played the piano properly — around the dead F. The last time she played it right in front of anybody was a November, four years ago. If you play well, she says, people ask you to play. Reading *New Moon* out of spite. Friday she signed the Manhattan Declaration from bed, with a cold. Two soups. She ate Julian’s. Mine’s on the sill for tomorrow. Ate Gloria’s soup cold out of the quart, at the sill, at six in the morning. Argued YES: a promise is made to a person, not to a reason. Wrote on my paper that I don’t believe one sentence of it. Neither does she. Mémère is lighting a candle for Nonna — the whole name. Half a name is half a candle.

body: Theo drove, with the top up for once, and Gloria’s box rode on Jack’s knees from the Anacapa lot to the airport with its string knotted twice. The coast was still black on the right when they started. Somewhere down the empty stretch of it the hills came apart from the sky — a line first, then a ridge, then a ridge with oaks on it — and Jack watched it happen and was thinking about her mouth. He had been thinking about it since the lot. He thought about it through Goleta. Theo drove with both hands and the radio off.

Now the SL sits in long-term parking, nose out, between a minivan and a Suburban, like a dare. The terminal is white stucco and red tile, built for some other decade’s idea of how many people fly, and on the Wednesday before Thanksgiving the line goes out the door and down the sidewalk: car seats, a soldier, a girl with a cello case, a man checking a turkey fryer in its original box.

Julian’s car is at the curb with its flashers going. Lena gets out in the cardigan with a duffel and a box of Kleenex, and Julian comes around and lifts her bag out of the trunk and sets it on the curb, and that’s as far as he’s allowed; a man in an orange vest is already waving the next car up.

body.text: Passing him, Theo glances at Jack first, and does it anyway, quieter. “Julian. Don’t write a song about the drive back.”
body.else: Theo, passing him with the boarding passes fanned in one hand, says, “Julian. Don’t write a song about the drive back.”

body: Julian smiles at the pavement. Jack, holding a pie, is in no position to stop anybody.
Lena looks at Theo’s bag — a leather weekender with somebody else’s initials on it — and at Jack. “Theo Vance is going to *Youngstown*?”
“I’ve been invited,” Theo says. “I intend to be a revelation.”
She looks from one of them to the other. Then she hands Theo her Kleenex to carry, as the price of the information.

The security line is shoes off and three ounces of anything in a quart bag. Lena stands behind Jack in her socks with her boots in one hand, the Justins, resoled twice, and goes around tomorrow’s table on Dupre Street for him chair by chair: Daddy carving, Josie biting somebody, her mother counting the chairs twice. She skips one chair. He lets her.
At the belt the pie goes through the X-ray in its white box between Jack’s boots and Lena’s, and the woman at the screen stops the belt and studies it for some time. “What kind?”
“Diplomatic,” says Theo, in his socks.

Past the checkpoint it’s one long room for everybody, the gates along the windows and the planes right out there on the apron with stairs rolled up to them, near enough to watch a pilot drink his coffee. Lena sits on her duffel and digs in her bag past her worship aid and a library book, and hands up a holy card: Our Lady of Prompt Succor, blue and gold, the Child on her arm, one corner bent. “For your nonna. She’s a New Orleans saint. She works fast.” On the back, in red, Lena has written *Carmela Rinaldi* and *St. Bernard’s, Breaux Bridge — O. Broussard*, so the saint will know who sent her.
Then she looks up at him properly, the first time this morning, and takes her time about it. “You look like you didn’t sleep.”
“I didn’t.”

She reaches up and taps the card in his hand, twice, on the saint. “Tell her it’s urgent. She likes urgent.” She sits back on the duffel. “Call me Thursday. After the pie. I want to hear Theo say *pop*.”
“I’ve been practicing,” Theo says.

Becca is at the next gate — Seattle, then Spokane — sitting on the carpet with her back against a pillar and her planner open on her knees, and when she sees him she’s up off the floor in one move. “You’re *flying*!”

Theo is perfect to her. He holds her coffee level while she goes through her bag, gives it back without a drop gone, and asks after Idaho as if it were a relative. What she finds is a holy card: St. Raphael, with his staff and his fish, walking a boy down a road.
“For her,” Becca says. “Father Osei read her name at the twelve-ten. I’m still allowed to pray for her, right?”
“You’re allowed,” Jack says.

body.text: “I’m telling Mom at the table tomorrow,” she says. “Then Facebook.”
Then her eyes go past his shoulder, across the gate area, to Lena on her duffel with her boarding pass in her lap, and Becca watches her and says nothing at all.

body: The RAZR rides in his shirt pocket the entire time she talks, and keeps quiet.

journal.title: Becca Lindell
journal.text: Coeur d’Alene. Seven siblings; wants seven or nine kids, odd numbers, for the tiebreaker. Can butcher a deer — elk too. Has pulled a calf, and it shows. Ran the beach cleanup like a cattle drive and put me on her team. Asked about the scar in the water. Told her mother the cleanup was a date, then asked me if it was. Wrote FRIDAY? on her clipboard, and meant it. Drives her brother Eli’s red Ranger; St. Isidore on the visor. Second date: Friday-night football. Knows downs. Prayed a Glory Be on fourth and one. Learned the First Way on the bleachers and said it back perfectly. Kissed my cheek so there’s no confusion. Third date was mine. I asked. I paid. The elephant seals at Piedras Blancas at sunset, in Kevin’s Odyssey. She knew what every one of them weighed. Nobody’s ever planned a thing for her, she says. She’s been praying for two in the morning. Named a hermit crab Thomas, after the First Way, and asked Fr. Osei whose blessing it was. Works the Marine Lab touch tank Thursday afternoons and Friday at six in the morning — that’s how she signed Thomas out. He’s home; she knows him by the chip in his shell. Mailed Rosie a birthday card with Thomas on it and six true facts on the back, to the address I gave her for her Christmas cards. She does them in October. Has a page on her clipboard for Wes. She’s been praying for him and Lena since September. Her eyes are gray. Brought a survival bag to the library for my midterm, with a clementine for Lena. Prays at two, like always. Took me to *Where the Wild Things Are* at the Rialto; her favorite line is the last one. My mother wrote her a thank-you note. Her list for Halloween says WE SHOULD MATCH!! It’s due Halloween. She says I look at her like homework. She says she’ll wait. Stuck on the touch tank all weekend while we were at Big Sur: the weekend volunteer has the swine flu. Asked me for the monks’ fruitcake for her Grandma Agnes — the only honest fruitcake in America. I handed in my homework six days early. St. Isidore and St. Maria: her first. Early, she said. Nobody’s early but her. Halloween: she sewed my costume out of a Rathdrum Feed & Seed sack. She was St. Maria de la Cabeza in Mrs. Fitch’s lace, with a water jug. Best Saint, by acclamation — a gold halo. Never won anything that wasn’t a heifer. Home at 11:40 for the six o’clock tank; the volunteer still has the flu. ‘Farmer.’ Theo’s birthday: huckleberry jam from her mother, for Theo — the Idaho gift. Next to his mother all night. ‘He’s *mine*. Since the beach cleanup.’ Toasted St. Martin de Porres: a dog and a cat and a mouse, one bowl. The Portolá steps, November 4th: her mom’s been calling me her boyfriend since September. She asked if she could tell her she’s right. I said yes. Her mom first, then Facebook. She flies home to Spokane the Wednesday before Thanksgiving. Her mother has named the turkey. She asked how I’m getting home. Greyhound. She frowned. Her mother sent a box: socks, cookies, two jars of huckleberry — JACK, and FOR THE CATHOLIC ROOMMATE. She offered me Daisy’s money. Six hundred and twelve dollars. It’s there, she says. Daisy doesn’t mind. Saturday, Ohio State in overtime: she gave me a photograph of the elephant seals in a frame she painted, every seal labeled with what it weighs. She’ll call during her dad’s grace on Thanksgiving so I can hear it. She wants to watch Michigan here, with me. ‘Someday I want to see your house. Is that okay to say?’ Ma wrote her. Three days after Christmas. Pittsburgh’s cheaper than Cleveland. She looked. Wednesday, in Eli’s truck, I told her. She said she did everything right, and she did. ‘It just isn’t the thing, is it.’ She asked me to leave it up on Facebook till she’s told her mom at the table. Thursday at two she texted. Still praying for me — not a girlfriend thing, she says. At the twelve-ten she turned around across the aisle at the sign of peace and held out her hand. At the airport, a week to the day: St. Raphael, for Nonna. Father Osei read the name at the twelve-ten, and she heard.
